# A mouse in the elevated plus maze {#sec-movement-mouse}

In this case study, we'll use [`movement`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/) to analyse a mouse navigating an [elevated plus maze (EPM)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevated_plus_maze)—a widely used behavioural assay for measuring anxiety in rodents.
Our goal is to quantify how much time the mouse spends in each region of the maze.

We assume you are already familiar with the `movement` dataset structure and the `movement` GUI, both introduced in @sec-movement-intro.

::: {.callout-note title="Using the right environment"}

If you are following along this chapter on your own computer,
make sure to run all code snippets with the `animals-in-motion-env` environment activated
(see [prerequisites @sec-install-movement]). This also applies to launching the
`movement` graphical user interface (@sec-movement-gui).

:::

```{python}
#| include: false
import xarray as xr

xr.set_options(
    display_expand_attrs=False,
    display_expand_coords=False,
    keep_attrs=True,
)
```

## The elevated plus maze

The EPM consists of two open arms and two closed arms (enclosed by walls) arranged in a plus shape, elevated above the ground.
Because of the general aversion of mice to open, exposed spaces, mice tend to prefer the closed arms of the maze.
The proportion of time spent in the open arms is therefore commonly used as a measure of anxiety-like behaviour: the more time spent in the open arms, the less anxious the mouse.

::: {.callout-note title="Acknowledgement"}
Thanks to Loukia Katsouri for sharing this dataset with us.
:::

Let's start by importing everything we'll need.
Besides the usual suspects, we will use four parts of the `movement` API:
[`movement.sample_data`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.sample_data.html) to fetch the data,
[`movement.filtering`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.filtering.html) to clean it,
[`movement.plots`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.plots.html) to visualise where the mouse spent its time,
and [`movement.roi`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.roi.html) to define and analyse regions of the maze.

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from movement import sample_data
from movement.filtering import filter_by_confidence, rolling_filter
from movement.plots import plot_occupancy
from movement.roi import compute_region_occupancy, load_rois
```

## Load and inspect the data

In @sec-movement-intro we loaded pose tracks from a file on disk.
Here we'll instead use one of `movement`'s [sample datasets](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/user_guide/input_output.html#target-sample-data)—a curated collection of tracking outputs from various species and software, which are downloaded on demand and cached under `~/.movement/data`.

We fetch the EPM dataset with
[`fetch_dataset()`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.sample_data.fetch_dataset.html),
passing `with_video=True` so that the associated video is downloaded as well—we'll need it later.

```{python}
ds = sample_data.fetch_dataset(
    "DLC_single-mouse_EPM.predictions.h5", with_video=True
)
ds
```

These are [DeepLabCut](https://www.mackenziemathislab.org/deeplabcut) predictions for a single mouse, with 8 keypoints tracked over roughly 10 minutes at 30 fps.

Along with the pose tracks, this sample dataset comes with a video and a still frame extracted from it.
Their paths are stored as attributes of the dataset:

```{python}
print(ds.frame_path)
print(ds.video_path)
```

Take note of these paths—we'll need them when we draw regions of interest in the GUI.

## Clean the data

Pose estimation output inevitably contains low-confidence or erroneous predictions, especially around occluded body parts.
In this dataset the mouse is often partly hidden by the walls of the closed arms, so some cleaning is in order before we analyse its position.

We covered the tools for this in @sec-movement-intro, so this time you get to apply them yourself.

::: {.exercise-prompt}
Clean the pose tracks:

1. Discard predictions with a confidence score below `0.95`, using
   [`filter_by_confidence()`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.filtering.filter_by_confidence.html).
   Which keypoint loses the most data, and does that make sense given the maze?
2. Smooth the result with a rolling median filter, using
   [`rolling_filter()`](https://movement.neuroinformatics.dev/latest/api/movement.filtering.rolling_filter.html).

Call the cleaned position array `position_clean`—we'll use it for the rest of the chapter.
:::

::: {.exercise-solution}
```{python}
position_conf = filter_by_confidence(
    ds.position, ds.confidence, threshold=0.95, print_report=True
)

position_clean = rolling_filter(
    position_conf, window=5, statistic="median", min_periods=2
)
```

The `snout` is the worst affected, followed by `tail_end` and the two lateral keypoints.
These are the keypoints most likely to disappear behind the walls of the closed arms, or to be obscured when the mouse rears or grooms.
:::
